row.title: Special Marriage Act, 1954
row.section: Section 28: Divorce by mutual consent — the position in force
row.text:
Section 28 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 governs divorce by mutual consent.

Under section 28(1), a petition may be presented to the district court by both parties together on the ground that they have been living separately for a period of one year or more, that they have not been able to live together and that they have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved.

Under section 28(2), the motion for the decree is made by both parties not earlier than six months after the date of the presentation of the petition and not later than eighteen months after that date. If the petition is not withdrawn in the meantime, the court, on being satisfied after hearing the parties, passes a decree declaring the marriage dissolved with effect from the date of the decree. Six months is the cooling-off period before the second motion. Eighteen months is the last date for it.

The periods in section 28(2) were last fixed by the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976 (Act 68 of 1976), section 29, in force from 27 May 1976. No later amendment has changed them, and the passages in this index reproduce the text now in force.

The six-month period is directory, not mandatory. A court may waive it on an application made after the first motion, on the principles in Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746: the parties have already lived separately for a year or more, mediation and conciliation have failed, alimony and custody are settled, and the wait would only prolong distress. The waiver is in the court's discretion and is decided case by case.

row.title: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
row.section: Section 13B: Divorce by mutual consent — the position in force
row.text:
Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 governs divorce by mutual consent.

Under section 13B(1), a petition may be presented to the district court by both parties together on the ground that they have been living separately for a period of one year or more, that they have not been able to live together and that they have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved.

Under section 13B(2), the motion for the decree is made by both parties not earlier than six months after the date of the presentation of the petition and not later than eighteen months after that date. If the petition is not withdrawn in the meantime, the court, on being satisfied after hearing the parties, passes a decree of divorce with effect from the date of the decree. Six months is the cooling-off period before the second motion. Eighteen months is the last date for it.

Section 13B was inserted by the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976 (Act 68 of 1976), section 7, in force from 27 May 1976, with these periods as enacted. No later amendment has changed them, and the passages in this index reproduce the text now in force.

The six-month period is directory, not mandatory (Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) 8 SCC 746). A court may waive it on an application made about a week after the first motion where the one-year separation is already complete, mediation and conciliation have failed, alimony and custody are settled, and the wait would only prolong distress. In Amit Kumar v. Suman Beniwal (2023) 17 SCC 648 the Supreme Court held that these factors are illustrative and not exhaustive, and that the waiver remains in the court's discretion.
